title: TCAD Cryogenic Model Parameters Calibration based on 65 nm NMOS Experimental Data
summary: In this paper, 65 nm n-type Metal-Oxide-Semiconductor Field-Effect-Transistors (nMOSFETs) are taped out and measured at 292 K to 4.5 K. Technology Computer-Aided-Design (TCAD) model parameters are then calibrated to fit the simulation curves to experimental electrical curves. Transmission electron microscopy (TEM) is used to unveil the dimensions of the transistors to ensure accurate modeling. The experimental and simulation capacitance-voltage (CV) curves, drain current - gate voltage (IDVG) curves, and drain current - drain voltage (IDVD) curves are fitted well using the calibrated parameters. The major models calibrated are the Lucent model, which is comprised of an extended PhuMob model, Lombardi model for surface mobility, and the Hänsch high field mobility model. A band-tail model with adjusted band width is applied to fit the sub-threshold swings at all temperatures. The calibrated parameters are expected to be applicable to other technologies because TCAD models are not technology-specific. It is also found that, except for saturation velocity, no new temperature-dependent model is needed. The calibration process and fitting strategies are detailed and are expected to be applicable to calibrate other transistor types.

AI.tldr: This paper presents the tape-out and measurement of 65 nm nMOSFETs from 292 K down to 4.5 K, followed by TCAD model calibration using TEM-derived device dimensions. The calibrated Lucent mobility model (extended PhuMob, Lombardi surface mobility, Hänsch high-field model) and a band-tail model with adjusted bandwidth successfully reproduce CV, IDVG, and IDVD curves across all temperatures. The calibrated parameters are expected to be transferable to other technologies, and no additional temperature-dependent models are needed except for saturation velocity.
AI.motivation: To enable accurate cryogenic device modeling for 65 nm technology (and potentially other nodes) by calibrating TCAD parameters against measured experimental data across a wide temperature range from room temperature down to 4.5 K.
AI.method: 65 nm nMOSFETs are fabricated and measured at 292 K to 4.5 K. TEM is used to extract actual device dimensions for accurate modeling. TCAD model parameters are calibrated to fit experimental CV, IDVG, and IDVD curves. The Lucent model (combining extended PhuMob, Lombardi surface mobility, and Hänsch high-field models) and a band-tail model with adjusted bandwidth are used to reproduce sub-threshold swings at all temperatures.
AI.result: The calibrated simulation curves fit the experimental CV, IDVG, and IDVD characteristics well across the full 4.5 K–292 K temperature range. It was found that no new temperature-dependent models are required except for saturation velocity, and the calibrated parameters are technology-agnostic in principle.
AI.conclusion: The calibration process and fitting strategies are detailed and expected to be applicable to other transistor types and technologies, providing a foundation for cryogenic transistor modeling in TCAD.

title: A discrete duality finite volume method with harmonic average for semiconductor drift-diffusion equations
summary: The stationary drift-diffusion model is widely used to model charge transport in semiconductor devices. Classical methods, such as the finite volume Scharfetter--Gummel (FVSG) method, perform well on high-quality Delaunay meshes but struggle on irregular or distorted meshes due to their reliance on Voronoi diagrams. To overcome this mesh limitation, this article introduces a new approach that integrates harmonic average stabilization into the discrete duality finite volume method (DDFV-HA). To validate our scheme, we compare DDFV-HA and FVSG for semiconductor simulations on both high- and low-quality meshes. Experiments show that DDFV-HA matches FVSG on high-quality meshes and is more reliable and accurate on low-quality meshes. Applying DDFV-HA to a real-world thyristor further confirms that it is well-suited for semiconductor simulations in complex, irregular domains where high-quality meshes are not easy to generate.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces a new discrete duality finite volume method with harmonic average stabilization (DDFV-HA) for solving the stationary drift-diffusion model of charge transport in semiconductor devices. Unlike the classical finite volume Scharfetter-Gummel (FVSG) method that struggles on irregular or distorted meshes due to Voronoi diagram reliance, DDFV-HA performs reliably and accurately on low-quality meshes while matching FVSG on high-quality meshes, as validated by comparisons and a real-world thyristor simulation.
AI.motivation: Classical methods like the finite volume Scharfetter-Gummel (FVSG) method rely on Voronoi diagrams and perform poorly on irregular or distorted meshes, which are difficult to avoid in real-world semiconductor devices with complex geometries. A new scheme is needed that can handle low-quality meshes without sacrificing accuracy.
AI.method: The proposed approach integrates harmonic average stabilization into the discrete duality finite volume method (DDFV-HA) to solve the stationary drift-diffusion model for semiconductor charge transport.
AI.result: Experiments show DDFV-HA matches FVSG accuracy on high-quality meshes and outperforms FVSG in reliability and accuracy on low-quality meshes. Application to a real-world thyristor device confirms its suitability for semiconductor simulations in complex, irregular domains.
AI.conclusion: DDFV-HA is a robust alternative to FVSG for semiconductor simulations, particularly well-suited for complex, irregular domains where generating high-quality meshes is difficult.

title: Using Diffusion Models to Estimate Uncertainties in Analytic Continuation
summary: Inverse problems are ubiquitous in physics, chemistry, and engineering, arising when reconstructing hidden quantities from indirect measurements. A key example is the analytic continuation of imaginary-time correlation functions (iTCFs) to the real-frequency domain. This process requires an inverse Laplace transform, which is inherently ill-posed and highly sensitive to small input variations. Recent neural network (NN)-based methods have shown promising results by learning mappings from imaginary-time to real-frequency spectra, often outperforming traditional techniques such as maximum entropy. However, because the problem is ill-posed, many spectra fit the same iTCF. Regression-based approaches output a single solution, which approximates an average over the true solution space, and therefore fail to capture the full distribution of plausible power spectra. To address this issue, we introduce a diffusion-based framework for analytic continuation that learns the distribution of spectra consistent with a given iTCF. It offers two key advantages. First, it quantifies uncertainty directly from the learned distribution. Second, by analyzing the spread and structure of this distribution, we can quantitatively assess the intrinsic hardness of each inversion problem. We measure this hardness with a new metric, the uncertainty pseudo-volume. Applying the framework to an iTCF from a path-integral molecular dynamics simulation of liquid parahydrogen, we obtain the self-diffusion coefficient with an error bar and flag a secondary high-frequency peak as a possible spurious artifact. In contrast to previous attempts at uncertainty quantification, our generative approach rests on a concrete probabilistic basis, providing a more theoretically grounded measure of confidence in the reconstructed power spectra.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces a diffusion-based generative framework for analytic continuation of imaginary-time correlation functions, which learns the full distribution of plausible power spectra rather than a single regression output. This enables direct uncertainty quantification and a new hardness metric (uncertainty pseudo-volume) to assess the intrinsic difficulty of each inversion problem.
AI.motivation: Analytic continuation of iTCFs is ill-posed—many spectra fit the same iTCF—yet regression-based neural network methods output a single solution approximating an average, failing to capture the full distribution of plausible power spectra and lacking principled uncertainty quantification.
AI.method: A diffusion-based generative framework that learns the distribution of spectra consistent with a given imaginary-time correlation function. The learned distribution enables direct uncertainty quantification and a new quantitative metric, the uncertainty pseudo-volume, to assess the intrinsic hardness of each inversion problem.
AI.result: Applied to an iTCF from a path-integral molecular dynamics simulation of liquid parahydrogen, the framework yields the self-diffusion coefficient with an error bar and flags a secondary high-frequency peak as a potential spurious artifact.
AI.conclusion: Unlike previous uncertainty quantification attempts, this generative approach rests on a concrete probabilistic basis, offering a more theoretically grounded measure of confidence in reconstructed power spectra.

title: Learned proposals in trans-dimensional inference are optimal at equilibrium, not during assembly
summary: Inferring the dimension of a model - the number of components needed to explain data - jointly with the parameters is a pervasive problem, from counting sources in an image to mixture modeling, and reversible-jump Markov chain Monte Carlo solves it exactly but mixes slowly. Learned proposals are well established at fixed dimension, but whether they can accelerate the dimension-changing moves themselves has remained largely untested. We show that the answer has a structural origin: the optimal proposal for the dimension-changing birth move is a different object in different phases of the run. While the fit is being assembled it must match the current residual - a state-dependent quantity no state-independent network can represent - but at equilibrium it degenerates to the posterior's single-component marginal, which is exactly the distribution an adaptive normalizing flow learns from the sampler's own history. A learned state-independent birth proposal is therefore useless in one phase and optimal in the other. Controlled experiments confirm the attribution: applied with an exact Metropolis--Hastings correction that leaves the target invariant for any network, the learned births leave acceptance rates unchanged yet accelerate model-order mixing - in a ten-seed benchmark they meet a pre-specified stopping rule in six of ten runs, typically several times sooner, where a strong hand-tuned baseline meets it in one (one-sided p=0.03) - and an isolation experiment shows the same flow deployed within-model buys nothing. Making no domain-specific assumptions, the same sampler counts sources in a noisy image and reconstructs signals across scientific domains, including gravitational waves from ground- and space-based detectors and a scalp EEG recording. We release the method as HyperWave, an open-source package.

AI.tldr: This paper shows that learned proposals for dimension-changing (birth) moves in reversible-jump MCMC have a structural phase-dependent role: they are useless during the fitting phase (where the optimal proposal must match a state-dependent residual) but optimal at equilibrium (where it reduces to the posterior's single-component marginal, learnable by an adaptive normalizing flow). Controlled experiments confirm learned births accelerate model-order mixing while leaving acceptance rates unchanged, and the method generalizes across domains including noisy image source counting, gravitational waves, and EEG.
AI.motivation: Inferring model dimension jointly with parameters is pervasive (source counting, mixture modeling). Reversible-jump MCMC solves it exactly but mixes slowly. Learned proposals are well-established at fixed dimension, but whether they can accelerate dimension-changing moves had remained largely untested.
AI.method: The authors analyze the optimal proposal for the dimension-changing birth move and show it is different across run phases: state-dependent during assembly (matching the current residual) and degenerating to the posterior's single-component marginal at equilibrium. They use an adaptive normalizing flow that learns this marginal from the sampler's own history as a state-independent birth proposal, combined with an exact Metropolis-Hastings correction that leaves the target invariant for any network. They also perform an isolation experiment deploying the same flow within-model to test whether the benefit comes from within-model acceleration.
AI.result: In a ten-seed benchmark, learned births meet a pre-specified stopping rule in six of ten runs (typically several times sooner) versus one of ten for a strong hand-tuned baseline (one-sided p=0.03), while acceptance rates remain unchanged. The isolation experiment shows the same flow within-model buys nothing, confirming the effect is specific to dimension-changing moves. The sampler counts sources in noisy images and reconstructs gravitational wave signals from ground- and space-based detectors and scalp EEG, with no domain-specific assumptions.
AI.conclusion: Learned state-independent birth proposals are structurally phase-dependent: useless in the fitting phase but optimal at equilibrium. This provides a principled explanation for why learned dimension-changing proposals work, and the method (released as HyperWave, an open-source package) achieves accelerated model-order mixing across diverse scientific domains.

title: Modeling Bond-Dependent Kitaev-like interaction in 2D Edge-Sharing Tetrahedral Magnets: FeX (X=Te, Se)
summary: Bond-dependent magnetic interactions, exemplified by the Kitaev model, are known to arise from the interplay between spin-orbit coupling(SOC) and specific coordination geometries, yet their existence has so far been predominantly associated with edge-sharing octahedral systems. Whether analogous interactions survive in edge- sharing tetrahedral environments - relevant to iron-based superconductor parent compounds - remains an open question. Here, we construct a Kitaev-like model for monolayer FeTe and FeSe and demonstrate the presence of a previously unrecognized bond-dependent Ising-type interaction, induced jointly by chalcogen-mediated SOC and the tetrahedral crystal-field geometry. By mapping the first-principles calculations derived magnetic anisotropy energy mapping across representative linear magnetic orders, we disentangle the bond-dependent contributions from single-ion anisotropy. We reveal that the Kitaev-like interaction dominates the magnetic anisotropy in FeTe, whereas in FeSe, it fiercely competes with a single-ion anisotropy of opposite sign. The resulting noncollinear local anisotropy axes generate intrinsic single-site spin frustration, providing a microscopic mechanism for magnetic disorder beyond isotropic exchange models. Our results establish edge-sharing tetrahedral magnets as a new setting for bond-dependent interactions and extend the scope of Kitaev physics beyond octahedral coordination.

AI.tldr: This paper demonstrates the existence of bond-dependent Kitaev-like Ising interactions in edge-sharing tetrahedral magnets (monolayer FeTe and FeSe), induced jointly by chalcogen-mediated spin-orbit coupling and tetrahedral crystal-field geometry. The Kitaev-like interaction dominates magnetic anisotropy in FeTe but competes with single-ion anisotropy of opposite sign in FeSe, creating intrinsic single-site spin frustration.
AI.motivation: Bond-dependent magnetic interactions (Kitaev model) have so far been associated primarily with edge-sharing octahedral systems due to spin-orbit coupling and coordination geometry. Whether such interactions exist in edge-sharing tetrahedral environments—relevant to iron-based superconductor parent compounds—remains an open question. The authors aim to resolve this gap.
AI.method: The authors construct a Kitaev-like model for monolayer FeTe and FeSe. They perform first-principles calculations to derive magnetic anisotropy energy mappings across representative linear magnetic orders, disentangling bond-dependent contributions from single-ion anisotropy components.
AI.result: The Kitaev-like interaction dominates magnetic anisotropy in FeTe, while in FeSe it fiercely competes with a single-ion anisotropy of opposite sign. This competition produces noncollinear local anisotropy axes, generating intrinsic single-site spin frustration beyond isotropic exchange models.
AI.conclusion: Edge-sharing tetrahedral magnets represent a new setting for bond-dependent interactions, extending the scope of Kitaev physics beyond octahedral coordination. The findings provide a microscopic mechanism for magnetic disorder in iron-based materials that isotropic exchange models cannot capture.

title: Intermediate scattering function of Brownian particles in a tilted cosine potential
summary: We solve the Fokker-Planck equation for a Brownian particle in a tilted cosine potential and derive the intermediate scattering function (ISF), which captures the full spatio-temporal dynamics of the system. The model consists of a single overdamped Brownian particle in one dimension. We derive a generalized ISF comprising two wave vectors to describe correlations in the periodic potential. Exploiting the periodicity via Bloch's theorem, we formulate the problem within a spectral-theoretical framework and numerically compute the corresponding eigenfunctions and eigenvalues, from which we obtain the ISF and the probability density. Using time-dependent perturbation theory, we expand the ISF and derive low-order moments, including the mean-square displacement, time-dependent diffusivity, skewness, and the non-Gaussian parameter. Our analytical results are validated by Brownian-dynamics simulations and analyzed focussing on different regimes of the tilting force. The results are compared to a harmonic approximation and the deterministic limit.

AI.tldr: The authors solve the Fokker-Planck equation for a Brownian particle in a tilted cosine potential, deriving the intermediate scattering function (ISF) that captures full spatio-temporal dynamics. Using Bloch's theorem and spectral theory, they compute eigenfunctions/eigenvalues numerically, and via time-dependent perturbation theory obtain low-order moments (mean-square displacement, diffusivity, skewness, non-Gaussian parameter). Results are validated with Brownian-dynamics simulations across different tilting-force regimes and compared with harmonic approximation and the deterministic limit.
AI.motivation: To fully characterize the spatio-temporal dynamics of a Brownian particle in a tilted periodic potential—a canonical model relevant to systems like Josephson junctions, superionic conductors, and molecular motors—by deriving an exact intermediate scattering function and related transport quantities that go beyond standard harmonic approximations.
AI.method: The Fokker-Planck equation is solved for a single overdamped Brownian particle in a tilted cosine potential. Bloch's theorem is exploited to exploit periodicity within a spectral-theoretical framework; eigenfunctions and eigenvalues are computed numerically. The ISF is generalized to include two wave vectors to capture periodic correlations. Time-dependent perturbation theory expands the ISF to derive low-order moments, including MSD, time-dependent diffusivity, skewness, and the non-Gaussian parameter. Validation is performed via Brownian-dynamics simulations.
AI.result: Analytical ISF and probability densities are obtained, with low-order moments (MSD, diffusivity, skewness, non-Gaussian parameter) derived via perturbation theory. All results are validated numerically by Brownian-dynamics simulations across different tilting-force regimes, and compared against a harmonic approximation and the deterministic limit.
AI.conclusion: The generalized two-wave-vector ISF within a spectral-theoretic framework provides a complete description of the spatio-temporal dynamics of a Brownian particle in a tilted cosine potential, with perturbatively derived moments validated across regimes; the approach offers a robust tool that supersedes harmonic and deterministic approximations.

title: Floquet Quasiparticle Poisoning of Frozonium
comment: Main text: 10 pages, 4 figures. Supplementary material: 4 pages
summary: Periodic driving can suppress the Josephson nonlinearity of a fluxonium superconducting circuit, producing a nearly harmonic Floquet spectrum at isolated freezing points [K. Lewellen et al., Newton 2, 100434 (2026)]. Here we show that this dynamically frozen behavior does not generically suppress quasiparticle-induced dissipation in the resulting frozonium circuit. We formulate quasiparticle processes in the frozonium using a Floquet framework and analyze both drive-assisted Cooper-pair breaking and tunneling of pre-existing quasiparticles. Pair generation is controlled by gap-breaking thresholds at high drive frequencies, while multiphoton resonances produce pronounced rate enhancements at lower frequencies. Quasiparticle tunneling exhibits connected resonance structures organized by the harmonic Floquet-Magnus spectrum near the freezing point, with resonant hybridization generating characteristic avoided crossings. Our results show that suitable operating regimes must balance dynamical freezing against quasiparticle loss and provide a framework for identifying experimental drive parameters away from harmful resonances.

AI.tldr: This paper analyzes quasiparticle-induced dissipation in dynamically frozen "frozonium" superconducting circuits, showing that periodic driving that suppresses Josephson nonlinearity does not generically suppress quasiparticle losses. Using a Floquet framework, the authors characterize drive-assisted Cooper-pair breaking and pre-existing quasiparticle tunneling, revealing resonance structures and rate enhancements that must be avoided in experimental operation.
AI.motivation: Periodic driving can dynamically freeze the fluxonium circuit into a nearly harmonic Floquet spectrum at isolated freezing points, which is promising for quantum information applications. However, whether this dynamical freezing also suppresses quasiparticle-induced dissipation—a major decoherence channel in superconducting circuits—remains an open question that is crucial for practical viability.
AI.method: The authors formulate quasiparticle processes in the "frozonium" circuit using a Floquet framework, analyzing two distinct mechanisms: (1) drive-assisted Cooper-pair breaking governed by gap-breaking thresholds at high drive frequencies and multiphoton resonances at lower frequencies, and (2) tunneling of pre-existing quasiparticles, which exhibits connected resonance structures organized by the harmonic Floquet-Magnus spectrum near the freezing point with characteristic avoided crossings from resonant hybridization.
AI.result: Drive-induced pair generation is controlled by gap-breaking thresholds at high frequencies, while multiphoton resonances cause pronounced rate enhancements at lower frequencies. Quasiparticle tunneling displays connected resonance structures tied to the Floquet-Magnus spectrum, with resonant hybridization generating avoided crossings. The dynamical freezing does not generically suppress quasiparticle dissipation.
AI.conclusion: Suitable operating regimes for frozonium circuits must balance dynamical freezing against quasiparticle-induced loss. The framework provides a means to identify experimental drive parameters that avoid harmful resonances, guiding practical implementation of dynamically frozen fluxonium devices.

title: Vertical Gallium Oxide Isolated Source Electrode Field Effect Transistors (ISEFET) Without Planarization or Mid-Gap Acceptor Blocking Layers
summary: We propose and demonstrate the first vertical Gallium oxide device architecture without the use of planarization etch back processes or mid-gap acceptor regions. The Isolated Source Electrode Field Effect Transistor (ISEFET) incorporates a dielectric blocking layer to access an isolated source pad extending from the top fin metal. Scaled multi-fin channels were formed by electron beam lithography with a width of 200 nm along with the source pads and then etched to a trench depth of ~1.2 um. The fabricated devices showed enhancement mode operation with threshold voltage of 2 V and on-off ratio > 1e7 with excellent gate modulation characteristics. The resulting device proved to be comparable to existing vertical transistors and suitable for high-throughput prototyping and large-scale manufacturing of future Gallium oxide and other wide bandgap semiconductor devices.

AI.tldr: This paper presents the first vertical Gallium oxide (Ga2O3) device architecture without planarization etch-back or mid-gap acceptor regions. The proposed Isolated Source Electrode Field Effect Transistor (ISEFET) uses a dielectric blocking layer for source isolation and scaled multi-fin channels (200 nm width, ~1.2 μm depth) fabricated via electron beam lithography, achieving enhancement-mode operation with a threshold voltage of 2 V and on-off ratio exceeding 1e7.
AI.motivation: To overcome manufacturing challenges in vertical Ga2O3 devices by eliminating the need for planarization etch-back processes and mid-gap acceptor regions, enabling simpler fabrication suitable for large-scale manufacturing.
AI.method: A novel ISEFET architecture is introduced featuring a dielectric blocking layer to access an isolated source pad extending from the top fin metal. Scaled multi-fin channels (200 nm wide) and source pads are defined using electron beam lithography, followed by etching to a trench depth of ~1.2 μm.
AI.result: The fabricated ISEFETs demonstrated enhancement-mode operation with a threshold voltage of 2 V and on-off ratio greater than 1e7, with excellent gate modulation characteristics, comparable to existing vertical transistors.
AI.conclusion: The proposed ISEFET architecture is viable for high-throughput prototyping and large-scale manufacturing of future Ga2O3 and other wide bandgap semiconductor vertical devices, offering a simplified fabrication pathway without planarization or acceptor regions.

title: Predissociation dynamics of charged long-range Rydberg molecules
summary: We investigate predissociation in homonuclear ($^{87}$Rb$^*$$^{87}$Rb$^+$) and heteronuclear ($^{87}$Rb$^*$$^{7}$Li$^+$) long-range Rydberg atom-ion molecules. Owing to their micron-scale bond lengths, these dissociate on time scales far removed from those of more tightly bound diatomic molecules. We employ the eigenchannel $R$-matrix method to compute predissociation rates for a broad range of principal quantum numbers $n$. The rates depend strongly on the mass, but more remarkably display a rapid and periodic variation as a function of $n$ as well as within a single vibrational ladder. A semiclassical Landau-Zener-Stückelberg analysis reveals that Stückelberg interference governs the decay process and produces the observed variation in the molecular lifetime. Although the heavy mass of the homonuclear Rb molecule constrains its predissociation rates to a sub-kHz level, the lighter molecule $^{87}$Rb$^*$$^{7}$Li$^+$ dissociates on time scales competitive with radiative and collisional decay. This can enable in situ study of non-adiabatic decay via ion microscopy.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates predissociation in long-range Rydberg atom-ion molecules (both homonuclear 87Rb*87Rb+ and heteronuclear 87Rb*7Li+) using the eigenchannel R-matrix method. The predissociation rates show strong mass dependence and rapid periodic variation with principal quantum number n, explained by Stückelberg interference via a semiclassical Landau-Zener-Stückelberg analysis. The homonuclear Rb molecule has sub-kHz rates due to its heavy mass, while the lighter 87Rb*7Li+ molecule dissociates on time scales competitive with radiative and collisional decay, enabling in situ study of non-adiabatic decay via ion microscopy.
AI.motivation: To understand predissociation dynamics in long-range Rydberg atom-ion molecules, whose micron-scale bond lengths lead to dissociation time scales very different from tightly bound diatomic molecules, and to determine whether such molecules can be experimentally studied.
AI.method: The authors employ the eigenchannel R-matrix method to compute predissociation rates across a broad range of principal quantum numbers n for both homonuclear (87Rb*87Rb+) and heteronuclear (87Rb*7Li+) long-range Rydberg atom-ion molecules. They supplement this with a semiclassical Landau-Zener-Stückelberg analysis to interpret the observed rate variations.
AI.result: Predissociation rates depend strongly on mass and display rapid, periodic variation as a function of n and within a single vibrational ladder. The homonuclear 87Rb molecule has sub-kHz predissociation rates due to its heavy mass, whereas 87Rb*7Li+ dissociates on time scales competitive with radiative and collisional decay.
AI.conclusion: Stückelberg interference governs the decay process and produces the observed variation in molecular lifetime. The lighter heteronuclear molecule's competitive dissociation time scales make it amenable to in situ study of non-adiabatic decay via ion microscopy.

title: Diffusion and Solvation Dynamics of Ions in Water: Beyond the Brownian Approximation
comment: 27 pages total, including 4 pages of Supplementary Information; 7 figures (6 main, 1 supplementary) and 7 tables (including 5 supplementary)
summary: The coupled dynamics of ions and water molecules in their first hydration shell impact a variety of processes including ion diffusion, selective ion transport in water-filled nanopores, and the kinetics of ion-pairing, ion adsorption, and metal-ligand binding reactions. In this work, we study these coupled dynamics for alkali metals (Li, Na, K, Rb, Cs), alkaline Earth metals (Mg, Ca, Sr, Ba), and chloride through the lens of their dependence on ion isotopic mass. Results are validated against previous measurements of the isotopic mass-dependence of ion diffusion coefficients in water and previous ab initio calculations of ion high-frequency dynamics in water. We find that the vibrational power spectra of ions in water consistently exhibit either two or three peaks, i.e., ions have several rattling frequencies within their solvations shells as previously reported for a subset of the species examined here. These frequencies have different sensititivies to isotopic mass that may serve as signatures of ion solvation processes (such as the tendency of ions to orient their first-shell water molecules) and that also may relate to Hofmeister-like effects including the relative affinity of different metals for ribonucleic acid (RNA).

AI.tldr: This paper investigates the coupled dynamics of ions and water molecules in the first hydration shell for alkali metals, alkaline Earth metals, and chloride, focusing on how these dynamics depend on ion isotopic mass. The study finds that ion vibrational power spectra in water consistently show two or three peaks (rattling frequencies) with different sensitivities to isotopic mass, which may serve as signatures of solvation processes and relate to Hofmeister-like effects including metal affinity for RNA.
AI.motivation: The coupled dynamics of ions and water molecules in the first hydration shell impact many fundamental processes including ion diffusion, selective ion transport in nanopores, and kinetics of ion-pairing, adsorption, and metal-ligand binding. Understanding these dynamics through the lens of isotopic mass dependence provides a new perspective on ion solvation behavior.
AI.method: The study examines the isotopic mass-dependence of ion dynamics for alkali metals (Li, Na, K, Rb, Cs), alkaline Earth metals (Mg, Ca, Sr, Ba), and chloride. Results are validated against previous measurements of isotopic mass-dependence of ion diffusion coefficients in water and previous ab initio calculations of ion high-frequency dynamics in water.
AI.result: Ion vibrational power spectra in water consistently exhibit either two or three peaks, representing multiple rattling frequencies within solvation shells. These frequencies show different sensitivities to isotopic mass, which may serve as signatures of ion solvation processes and relate to Hofmeister-like effects, including the relative affinity of different metals for ribonucleic acid (RNA).
AI.conclusion: The rattling frequencies of ions in water have distinct isotopic mass sensitivities that can act as signatures of ion solvation behavior, particularly regarding the orientation of first-shell water molecules, and may be connected to Hofmeister-like effects such as differential metal affinity for RNA.

title: Graph-theoretic design of lasing networks for physical vision
summary: Physical neural networks perform learning through the intrinsic nonlinear dynamics of matter. Optimising their design presents a considerable challenge: complex many-body physics can provide powerful computation, but are expensive to simulate and large experimental optimisation runs are impractical to fabricate. Hence, the high-dimensional space of possible network topologies cannot be effectively directly searched. Here, we show that this search can be efficiently performed in an abstract graph space that is vastly cheaper to explore. Using random lasing networks -- composed of interconnected nanoscale waveguides and hosting strongly coupled lasing modes -- as an exemplar physical vision system, we establish a quantitative three-layer link: simple graph-theoretic metrics predict the nonlinear lasing physics, which in turn predicts vision performance. After validating this relationship using physical simulations, we exploit it to drive an evolutionary algorithm using graph metrics, producing network topologies that outperform random designs at a fraction of the computational cost (3000$\times$ speed-up compared to physical simulation). On simulated image-classification tasks, graph-optimised networks substantially improve classification accuracy. As our framework operates on network topology rather than substrate-specific physics, we anticipate it can transfer to other network-based physical learning systems, providing an efficient route for the directed design and optimisation of complex, strongly-interacting physical neural networks.

AI.tldr: The paper demonstrates that physical neural networks (using random lasing networks as an example) can be efficiently optimized by searching in an abstract graph space rather than simulating expensive physical dynamics. Simple graph-theoretic metrics predict nonlinear lasing physics, which in turn predicts vision performance, enabling a 3000× computational speed-up and improved classification accuracy.
AI.motivation: Optimizing physical neural networks is extremely challenging because the high-dimensional space of possible network topologies cannot be directly searched — simulations of complex many-body physics are expensive and large experimental optimization runs are impractical.
AI.method: The authors establish a three-layer quantitative link: graph-theoretic metrics → nonlinear lasing physics → vision performance. They validate this relationship with physical simulations, then use graph metrics to drive an evolutionary algorithm that generates network topologies without requiring physical simulation.
AI.result: The graph-driven evolutionary algorithm produces network topologies that outperform random designs with a 3000× speed-up over physical simulation. On simulated image-classification tasks, graph-optimized networks substantially improve classification accuracy.
AI.conclusion: Since the framework operates on network topology rather than substrate-specific physics, it can transfer to other network-based physical learning systems, providing an efficient route for directed design and optimization of complex, strongly-interacting physical neural networks.

title: Mechanisms of Nanoscroll Formation and Particle Encapsulation in Janus MXenes
comment: This is a preprint submitted to a journal for publication
summary: Morphology transfer of 2D Janus MXenes into nanoscrolls unlocks unusual properties. Although a scalable synthesis route has been experimentally verified, the atomistic mechanism underlying nanoscroll formation remains poorly understood. We use large-scale reactive molecular dynamics simulations, validated against density functional theory (DFT) and experimental structural and elastic properties, to investigate stability and quantify the driving forces and geometry governing nanoscroll formation in three Janus MXenes, (Tx)Ti2C(Ty), where (Tx) and (Ty) denote the bottom and top surface terminations among bare (-b), -O, and -OH. Both square and infinitely wide flakes with lengths ranging from 10 to over 120 nm are simulated. We find that 1-7% lattice-induced strain generates a bending moment in these structures. The sheet scrolls, curves, or forms a nanotube depending on the resulting curvature and initial sheet size. For MXenes with an initial length of 120 nm, multiwalled nanoscrolls form with interlayer distances of around 0.7 nm and inner diameters of about 7 nm for (O)Ti2C(OH) and (b)Ti2C(OH), whereas (b)Ti2C(O) instead produces a much larger interlayer distance of around 1.7 nm and an inner diameter exceeding 20 nm. We show that spontaneous scrolling of a Janus MXene in the presence of an anchored nanoparticle produces a core@shell composite, in which the particle locally deforms the nanoscroll and widens the interlayer channels. This locally tunable, enlarged interlayer spacing offers a promising design route for MXene-based energy-storage electrodes. However, our simulations reveal H2 gas release during encapsulation, which promotes nanobubble formation that can reduce battery life.

AI.tldr: This paper uses large-scale reactive molecular dynamics simulations (validated against DFT and experiments) to uncover the atomistic mechanisms driving nanoscroll formation in Janus MXenes (Tx)Ti2C(Ty) with varying surface terminations. The simulations reveal that 1-7% lattice-induced strain creates a bending moment causing sheets to scroll, curve, or form nanotubes. Multiwalled nanoscrolls form with interlayer distances of ~0.7 nm for (O)Ti2C(OH) and (b)Ti2C(OH), while (b)Ti2C(O) yields larger spacings (~1.7 nm). Spontaneous scrolling around anchored nanoparticles produces core@shell composites with locally enlarged interlayer channels, offering a design route for energy-storage electrodes, though H2 release during encapsulation promotes nanobubble formation that can reduce battery life.
AI.motivation: Although a scalable synthesis route for 2D Janus MXene nanoscrolls has been experimentally verified, the atomistic mechanism underlying nanoscroll formation remains poorly understood. Understanding this mechanism is critical for enabling rational design and optimization of these materials for applications such as energy storage.
AI.method: Large-scale reactive molecular dynamics simulations, validated against density functional theory (DFT) and experimental structural and elastic properties, are used to investigate stability and quantify the driving forces and geometry governing nanoscroll formation in three Janus MXenes: (Tx)Ti2C(Ty) with bottom and top surface terminations among bare (-b), -O, and -OH. Both square and infinitely wide flakes with lengths from 10 to over 120 nm are simulated.
AI.result: 1-7% lattice-induced strain generates a bending moment; the sheet scrolls, curves, or forms a nanotube depending on curvature and initial size. For 120 nm long flakes, multiwalled nanoscrolls form: (O)Ti2C(OH) and (b)Ti2C(OH) produce interlayer distances of ~0.7 nm and inner diameters of ~7 nm, while (b)Ti2C(O) yields ~1.7 nm interlayer distance and inner diameter exceeding 20 nm. Spontaneous scrolling around anchored nanoparticles yields core@shell composites with locally widened interlayer channels. However, H2 gas release during encapsulation promotes nanobubble formation that can reduce battery life.
AI.conclusion: Spontaneous scrolling of Janus MXenes around nanoparticles provides a locally tunable, enlarged interlayer spacing, offering a promising design route for MXene-based energy-storage electrodes. However, H2 gas release during encapsulation and resulting nanobubble formation present a challenge that can reduce battery life and must be addressed.

title: Quantum-Geometric Bound on Dynamical Instability in Bosonic Systems
summary: Quantum-geometric speed and dynamical instability are two natural rates for a driven quantum system, and their relation is unsettled even for exactly solvable dynamics. Here we show that for any multimode quadratic bosonic system referred to the bare-mode vacuum the Fubini-Study speed v_FS is the Frobenius norm of the symmetric, stretching part of the flow. This yields a sharp bound, lambda_max <= sqrt(2) v_FS, saturated by a resonant pure squeezer. The bound is not invertible: in a detuned parametric amplifier we hold either rate fixed while varying the other.

AI.tldr: The paper proves that for any multimode quadratic bosonic system, the Fubini-Study speed equals the Frobenius norm of the symmetric (stretching) part of the flow, yielding a sharp bound relating the maximum dynamical instability rate to the quantum-geometric speed. The bound is saturated by a resonant pure squeezer but is non-invertible, as demonstrated in a detuned parametric amplifier where each rate can be held fixed while varying the other.
AI.motivation: To resolve the long-standing unsettled relationship between the quantum-geometric speed (Fubini-Study speed) and dynamical instability (Lyapunov-type growth rate) in driven quantum systems, even for exactly solvable cases.
AI.method: The authors analyze any multimode quadratic bosonic system relative to the bare-mode vacuum, showing that the Fubini-Study speed v_FS is given by the Frobenius norm of the symmetric (stretching) part of the symplectic flow. From this they derive an inequality bound and analyze its saturation and invertibility properties via examples such as a resonant pure squeezer and a detuned parametric amplifier.
AI.result: The main result is the sharp bound λ_max ≤ √2 v_FS, where λ_max is the maximum dynamical instability rate, saturated exactly by a resonant pure squeezer. The bound is shown to be non-invertible: in a detuned parametric amplifier, one can hold either the geometric speed or the instability rate fixed while independently varying the other.
AI.conclusion: The quantum-geometric speed and dynamical instability are connected by a sharp but non-invertible bound for quadratic bosonic systems, clarified through the decomposition of the flow into stretching and rotation parts.

title: The "Moiré Capacitor Effect" and Stabilization of Fractional Chern Insulators in Rhombohedral Graphene Superlattices
summary: While the necessity of a moiré potential for fractional Chern insulators (FCIs) in rhombohedral graphene-hBN superlattices, first predicted in Ref. 1, is now grounded in experiments, a theory of its origin and importance remains at large. We present a mechanism---the moiré capacitor effect---that enhances the moiré potential by electrostatically imprinting the valence charge density onto the conduction bands. We derive the analytical form of this term and reveal its crucial role in stabilizing a parent state with Chern number $C=1$ at filling $ν=1$. We propose a parent state theory which posits that stability of the Chern insulator and flatness of its hole excitations are necessary for obtaining FCIs upon doping. We then perform multi-band exact diagonalization calculations to confirm the emergence of FCIs at $ν= 2/3$ in the presence of the moiré capacitor effect. Our FCI state is stabilized by inter-band fluctuations, unlike in the moire-free case which collapses with band-mixing. We provide the first consistent theory for this state in aligned samples and explain its absence in unaligned ones.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes the "moiré capacitor effect" as a mechanism that enhances the moiré potential in rhombohedral graphene-hBN superlattices by electrostatically imprinting valence charge density onto conduction bands. This effect stabilizes a C=1 parent state at filling ν=1 and enables fractional Chern insulators at ν=2/3, confirmed by multi-band exact diagonalization. The authors provide the first consistent theory explaining the presence of FCIs in aligned samples and their absence in unaligned ones.
AI.motivation: While experiments have established the necessity of a moiré potential for fractional Chern insulators (FCIs) in rhombohedral graphene-hBN superlattices, no theory yet explains its origin and why it is crucial. This work aims to fill that gap by providing a mechanism and analytical framework.
AI.method: The authors derive an analytical form of the moiré capacitor effect, which electrostatically imprints valence band charge density onto conduction bands. They propose a parent state theory requiring stability of the Chern insulator and flatness of its hole excitations for FCIs upon doping. They perform multi-band exact diagonalization calculations to test the emergence of FCIs at ν=2/3.
AI.result: The moiré capacitor effect enhances the moiré potential and is crucial for stabilizing a C=1 parent state at ν=1. Multi-band exact diagonalization confirms FCIs at ν=2/3, which are stabilized by inter-band fluctuations—unlike the moiré-free case that collapses with band mixing. This provides the first consistent theory for FCI emergence in aligned samples and explains their absence in unaligned ones.
AI.conclusion: The moiré capacitor effect is the key mechanism underlying the importance of the moiré potential for FCIs. The proposed parent state theory and exact diagonalization results provide a unified explanation for the experimental observation of FCIs in aligned rhombohedral graphene-hBN superlattices and their absence in unaligned samples.

title: Characteristic Mode Analysis of Plasmonic Nanostructures Using Hydrodynamic Volume Integral Equation
summary: Metallic nanostructures confine electromagnetic fields at subwavelength scales, making them attractive as plasmonic nanoantennas. At these scales, the response of metals becomes nonlocal, and the hydrodynamic model is widely used to capture this response. However, existing solvers provide only the response to a prescribed excitation and do not directly reveal the intrinsic resonances of the structure. This work extends the characteristic mode analysis to plasmonic nanostructures to enable excitation-independent modal analysis of their resonant behavior. For simple metals, the coupled hydrodynamic and volume integral equations are reduced to a single hydrodynamic volume integral equation in terms of the induced current. The equation is discretized and cast as a generalized eigenvalue problem within the characteristic mode analysis framework, whose solution yields the characteristic mode currents and modal significance curves of the structure. The proposed framework is validated through three metallic nanostructures: a nanosphere, a nanorod, and a nanodimer. The results show that the method identifies the intrinsic resonances of each structure, including resonances not excited by a given source and additional resonances arising from the nonlocal response, which are absent in local models. The proposed framework provides physical insight into the modal mechanisms of plasmonic nanostructures and serves as a practical tool for their analysis and design.

AI.tldr: This paper extends characteristic mode analysis (CMA) to plasmonic nanostructures by reducing coupled hydrodynamic and volume integral equations to a single hydrodynamic volume integral equation, enabling excitation-independent modal analysis that reveals intrinsic resonances, including those from nonlocal response effects.
AI.motivation: Existing solvers for plasmonic nanostructures only provide responses to prescribed excitations and cannot directly reveal the intrinsic resonances of the structure. With the hydrodynamic model capturing nonlocal response, there is a need for an excitation-independent modal analysis framework.
AI.method: The coupled hydrodynamic and volume integral equations are reduced to a single hydrodynamic volume integral equation in terms of induced current. The equation is discretized and formulated as a generalized eigenvalue problem within the characteristic mode analysis framework, yielding characteristic mode currents and modal significance curves.
AI.result: Validation on three metallic nanostructures (nanosphere, nanorod, nanodimer) shows the method identifies intrinsic resonances including those not excited by a given source and additional resonances arising from nonlocal response that are absent in local models.
AI.conclusion: The proposed framework provides physical insight into modal mechanisms of plasmonic nanostructures and serves as a practical tool for their analysis and design.

title: Thermodynamics of Learning: A Typed Four-Component Accounting of Memory, Fit, and Value
summary: What a finite learning device has recorded and what will hold value for it on future tasks are not the same quantity. We develop a typed accounting for finite-state learning devices that separates four components: a training-side fit functional $Φ_{\mathrm{fit}}$, the record-correlation stock $J_{D}=I(M;D)$, an update-side search ledger $σ_{M}$, and an operational capital value $V(M;T,b)$. This value is the work gap between an informed protocol class and a blind class obtained by deleting the memory-read port and re-optimizing from scratch. (I) Separation: for every $n$, there is a device family on which record correlation and world correlation grow by $n\ln 2$ while the capital gain is exactly zero. In the $\mathrm{flat}^{*}$ regime, data-free updates never increase $V$. (II) Capitalization ledger: an exact $\mathrm{flat}^{*}$ extraction identity and a universal ledger identity give, for (F5$'$)-stable $M$-local updates under a no-discarded-record-correlation condition (f), the bound $η_{\mathrm{cap}}\le 1$ for the capitalization efficiency $η_{\mathrm{cap}}=ΔV/(k T\,σ_{M})$, together with necessary and sufficient conditions for equality. (III) Value retention: for the retention gap $L_{\mathrm{gen}}$ and retention ratio $ρ_{\mathrm{gen}}$ (the former carries no sign constraint; the latter is defined for positive training-side value and is not confined to $[0,1]$) we give a two-layer alignment domain: an exact exchange rate between value and the side-information-adjusted record fit $I(M';D\mid Y)$ without any record-side-information independence assumption, and a raw record-stock exchange rate under a joint side-information neutrality condition $(M,D)\perp Y$, whose boundary is marked by an explicit one-time-pad witness. These are statements about finite-device value retention under task-distribution shift, not a theory of statistical generalization.

AI.tldr: The paper develops a typed accounting framework for finite-state learning devices that separates training-side fit, record-correlation stock, update-side search ledger, and operational capital value. It establishes separation results, capitalization ledger identities with efficiency bounds, and value retention guarantees under distribution shift.
AI.motivation: The key insight is that what a finite learning device has recorded is not the same as what holds value for future tasks. This distinction motivates a rigorous, quantitative accounting that separates different facets of a learning device's state to understand how recorded information translates (or fails to translate) into future value.
AI.method: The paper introduces four formal components: a training-side fit functional Φ_fit, record-correlation stock J_D = I(M;D), update-side search ledger σ_M, and operational capital value V(M;T,b) defined as the work gap between an informed protocol class and a blind class that deletes the memory-read port and re-optimizes. The analysis covers (I) separation via explicit device families, (II) capitalization ledgers via flat* extraction identities and universal ledger identities with stability conditions, and (III) value retention via two-layer alignment domains with exchange rates and side-information neutrality conditions.
AI.result: (I) Shows device families where record correlation and world correlation grow by n ln 2 yet capital gain is exactly zero; under flat* regime, data-free updates never increase V. (II) Establishes a capitalization efficiency bound η_cap ≤ 1 with necessary and sufficient conditions for equality under (F5')-stable M-local updates with no-discarded-record-correlation. (III) Provides exact exchange rates between value and side-information-adjusted record fit without independence assumptions, plus raw exchange rates under joint side-information neutrality, with an explicit one-time-pad witness marking the boundary.
AI.conclusion: The framework provides precise finite-device value retention statements under task-distribution shift. Key findings: recorded information can grow unboundedly without yielding capital gains, capitalization efficiency never exceeds 1 under specified stability and correlation conditions, and value retention can be quantified via exact exchange rates to record fit under mild alignment conditions. These are specifically about finite-device value retention, explicitly not a theory of statistical generalization.

title: Finite-momentum coupling of Higgs and Bardasis--Schrieffer modes in superconductors with competing pairing channels
summary: In superconductors with competing pairing channels, two well defined excitations exist below the pair-breaking edge: the Higgs mode of the condensed $s$-wave channel and the Bardasis--Schrieffer (BS) exciton of the subdominant $d$-wave channel. Their mixing is doubly forbidden --- by point-group symmetry at zero momentum and because the two reside in the amplitude and phase sectors of the order parameter respectively, by particle--hole symmetry at every momentum. Working in a Nambu--Keldysh quasiclassical framework extended to leading $1/\varepsilon_F$ corrections and including the self-consistently screened Coulomb potential, we show that finite momentum combined with particle--hole asymmetry generates a direct coupling which we obtain in closed form. Whether this coupling produces an avoided crossing is decided, however, not by its magnitude but by kinematics. In the clean limit the Higgs is not a sub-gap pole but a resonance pinned to the pair-breaking edge, which disperses with coefficient unity in $(v_Fq)^2$, while the bound BS mode disperses more slowly: the two branches therefore separate rather than converge and never become degenerate. The obstruction is specific to the clean limit: exact dirty-limit results show that disorder detaches the amplitude resonance from the edge and reverses its dispersion, which can result in an avoided crossing with the BS mode at intermediate scattering. In that regime, the coupling computed here would set the splitting between the hybridized branches. We discuss the experimental implications of these results.

AI.tldr: This paper studies the coupling between the Higgs mode (in the s-wave pairing channel) and the Bardasis-Schrieffer (BS) exciton (in the subdominant d-wave channel) in superconductors with competing pairing channels. While their mixing is doubly forbidden by point-group and particle-hole symmetry, the authors show that finite momentum plus particle-hole asymmetry generates a direct coupling. However, whether an avoided crossing occurs is determined by kinematics: in the clean limit, the two branches separate rather than converge. Only with disorder (in the dirty limit) does the amplitude resonance detach from the edge and reverse dispersion, potentially enabling an avoided crossing at intermediate scattering strengths.
AI.motivation: To determine whether the Higgs mode and Bardasis-Schrieffer exciton can hybridize in superconductors with competing pairing channels, despite being forbidden from mixing by both point-group symmetry (at zero momentum) and particle-hole symmetry (at every momentum). Understanding this coupling is important for interpreting experiments that probe collective excitations in unconventional superconductors.
AI.method: The authors work in a Nambu-Keldysh quasiclassical framework extended to leading 1/ε_F corrections, including the self-consistently screened Coulomb potential. They analytically derive a closed-form expression for the direct coupling between the Higgs mode and BS mode that arises from finite momentum combined with particle-hole asymmetry.
AI.result: The coupling is obtained in closed form, but whether it produces an avoided crossing is decided by kinematics rather than coupling magnitude. In the clean limit, the Higgs resonance remains pinned to the pair-breaking edge and disperses with coefficient unity in (v_F q)^2, while the BS mode disperses more slowly, so the branches separate rather than converge. In the dirty limit, disorder detaches the amplitude resonance from the edge and reverses its dispersion, enabling an avoided crossing at intermediate scattering rates; in that regime the computed coupling sets the splitting between hybridized branches.
AI.conclusion: The Higgs-BS coupling induced by finite momentum and particle-hole asymmetry is real but kinematically forbidden from producing an avoided crossing in the clean limit. Disorder can reverse the dispersion of the amplitude resonance, making hybridization possible at intermediate disorder strengths. The results have experimental implications for observing these collective modes.

title: Origin of effective non-Fourier heat conduction phenomena in heterogeneous materials
summary: Phenomenological models of non-Fourier heat conduction often lack a strict microstructural foundation, leading to ambiguities when modeling complex heterogeneous materials. In this study, we derive a continuum heat equation beyond Fourier's law using spatial volume averaging for a two-component system. We analytically prove that the experimentally observed static and dynamic thermal diffusivity arise directly from the distinct material properties, concluding that heterogeneous media are inherently over-diffusive. The resulting heat equation is thermodynamically compatible, and the microstructural origin allows the calculation of non-Fourier transport coefficients. Furthermore, we demonstrate that finite-sample boundaries introduce higher-order spatial non-localities, thereby explaining the size dependence of over-diffusion. We validate the model against experimental data across metal and carbon foams, rocks, and metal-organic frameworks.

AI.tldr: This paper derives a continuum heat equation beyond Fourier's law for heterogeneous two-component materials using spatial volume averaging, demonstrating that heterogeneous media are inherently over-diffusive and that finite-sample boundaries introduce higher-order non-localities explaining size-dependent over-diffusion. The model is thermodynamically compatible, provides microstructural origins for non-Fourier transport coefficients, and is validated against experiments on metal foams, carbon foams, rocks, and metal-organic frameworks.
AI.motivation: Phenomenological non-Fourier heat conduction models lack a strict microstructural foundation, causing ambiguities when modeling complex heterogeneous materials. The authors aim to provide a rigorously derived, microstructure-based continuum heat equation that resolves these ambiguities.
AI.method: The authors use spatial volume averaging to derive a continuum heat equation beyond Fourier's law for a two-component system. They analytically relate experimentally observed static and dynamic thermal diffusivity to the distinct material properties, and incorporate boundary effects to capture higher-order spatial non-localities.
AI.result: The study proves that heterogeneous media are inherently over-diffusive, derives a thermodynamically compatible heat equation, enables calculation of non-Fourier transport coefficients from microstructure, and explains size dependence of over-diffusion via finite-sample boundary effects. The model is validated against experimental data from metal and carbon foams, rocks, and metal-organic frameworks.
AI.conclusion: The derived heat equation provides a microstructurally grounded, thermodynamically consistent framework for non-Fourier heat conduction in heterogeneous materials, explaining over-diffusion and its size dependence, with broad experimental validation.

title: Precision Positronium Spectroscopy as a Test of the Helium Ionization Energy Anomaly
summary: Precise measurements of the metastable helium (1s)(2s)$\,^3S_1$ ionization energy have revealed a 9$σ$ discrepancy with QED theory that persists in isotopic measurements, suggesting a leptophilic bosonic interaction as a possible explanation. A subsequent investigation of such interactions has concluded that only a scalar boson interaction is consistent with the He observations. Taking this as a starting point, we derive the response of positronium energy levels to the corresponding finite-range Yukawa potential, using exact hydrogenic matrix elements and a numerical helium calculation. Across the viable mediator-mass range of 0-800 eV, the He anomaly interpreted in this way implies a positronium 1$^3$S$_1 \rightarrow 2^3$S$_1$ shift ranging from 0.250-0.850 MHz, and a 2S-ionization shift of 0.14-0.21 MHz. We discuss the feasibility of observing these shifts experimentally.

AI.tldr: The paper interprets a measured 9σ discrepancy between metastable helium ionization energy and QED theory as evidence for a leptophilic scalar boson interaction, and derives the corresponding predictions for positronium energy level shifts. It finds mediator-mass-dependent shifts of 0.250-0.850 MHz for the 1^3S_1→2^3S_1 transition and 0.14-0.21 MHz for the 2S-ionization shift, and evaluates experimental feasibility.
AI.motivation: A persistent 9σ discrepancy between measured metastable helium (2^3S) ionization energy and QED predictions, confirmed in isotopic measurements, suggests new physics such as a leptophilic bosonic interaction. Only a scalar boson was found consistent with the helium observations, motivating a study of its implications for positronium—a purely leptonic system well-suited for precision tests.
AI.method: The authors take the scalar-boson interpretation of the helium anomaly as a starting point and derive positronium energy level perturbations from a finite-range Yukawa potential. They use exact hydrogenic matrix elements for analytic treatment and a numerical helium calculation for consistency, scanning the viable mediator mass range of 0-800 eV.
AI.result: For mediator masses between 0-800 eV, the helium anomaly interpreted as a scalar boson interaction implies a positronium 1^3S_1→2^3S_1 shift of 0.250-0.850 MHz and a 2S-ionization shift of 0.14-0.21 MHz. The experimental observability of these shifts is discussed.
AI.conclusion: The helium anomaly, if due to a new leptophilic scalar boson, predicts measurable shifts in positronium fine and ionization transitions that are potentially within reach of current experimental sensitivity, offering an independent test of the new-physics interpretation.

title: Integrated Alchemical and Conformational Enhanced Sampling for Solvation Free Energy Calculations
summary: Accurate solvation free energies from molecular dynamics simulations require efficient sampling of coupled slow variables, including solvent coordinates, solute conformational modes, and the alchemical coordinate $λ$. Here, we develop a $λ$-dynamics framework that combines mass scaling, on-the-fly probability enhanced sampling (OPES), and driven adiabatic free energy dynamics (d-AFED) to address these sampling challenges within a unified protocol. For rigid organic solutes, Hamiltonian replica exchange with mass scaling is first used to quantify the effect of octanol solvent relaxation. Reducing all octanol atomic masses by a factor of ten accelerates convergence by more than fivefold while preserving equilibrium solvation free energies. These calculations then provide reference benchmarks for $λ$-OPES, a dual-bias $λ$-dynamics strategy that combines the "standard" and "explore" variants of OPES to promote transitions along the alchemical coordinate. This approach reaches convergence on timescales comparable to replica exchange, but without predefined $λ$ windows or multiple parallel simulations. For flexible $N$-acetyl amino-acid amide solutes, $λ$-OPES is coupled with d-AFED on selected backbone and side-chain dihedrals to enable simultaneous alchemical and conformational enhanced sampling. This combined strategy improves agreement with experimental octanol-water partition coefficients and reduces the mean absolute error from 0.75 log units with $λ$-OPES alone to 0.30 log units with $λ$-OPES-d-AFED. Overall, this work establishes an integrated enhanced sampling protocol for solvation free energy calculations across rigid organic solutes and flexible peptide-like solutes, and provides a foundation for the application of alchemical free energy methods to larger and more conformationally complex systems.

AI.tldr: This paper develops an integrated λ-dynamics enhanced sampling framework combining mass scaling, OPES (dual-bias standard+explore variants), and d-AFED to efficiently compute solvation free energies. For rigid solutes, mass-scaled Hamiltonian replica exchange quantifies octanol relaxation and achieves >5× convergence speedup; λ-OPES matches replica-exchange convergence without predefined windows. For flexible peptide-like solutes, coupling λ-OPES with d-AFED on dihedrals improves octanol-water partition coefficient agreement, reducing MAE from 0.75 to 0.30 log units.
AI.motivation: Accurate solvation free energies from MD simulations require efficient sampling of coupled slow variables (solvent coordinates, conformational modes, and the alchemical coordinate λ), which remains a major sampling challenge. The authors aim to develop a unified protocol that addresses all these coupled sampling bottlenecks simultaneously.
AI.method: The framework combines three techniques within a unified protocol: (1) mass scaling applied to octanol solvent atoms for Hamiltonian replica exchange to quantify solvent relaxation effects; (2) λ-OPES, a dual-bias λ-dynamics strategy merging the "standard" and "explore" OPES variants to enhance transitions along the alchemical coordinate without predefined windows; (3) d-AFED applied to selected backbone and side-chain dihedrals for flexible solutes, enabling simultaneous alchemical and conformational enhanced sampling (λ-OPES-d-AFED).
AI.result: Mass-scaling octanol atoms by 10× accelerates replica-exchange convergence by more than fivefold while preserving equilibrium solvation free energies. λ-OPES reaches convergence comparable to replica exchange without parallel simulations or predefined λ windows. For flexible N-acetyl amino-acid amides, λ-OPES-d-AFED reduces the mean absolute error for octanol-water partition coefficients from 0.75 log units (λ-OPES alone) to 0.30 log units.
AI.conclusion: This work establishes an integrated enhanced sampling protocol for solvation free energy calculations across both rigid organic solutes and flexible peptide-like solutes, and provides a foundation for applying alchemical free energy methods to larger, more conformationally complex systems.

title: Superconductivity in the $t$-$t'$ Hubbard Model from Symmetry-Preserving Neural-Network Quantum States
summary: Despite its fundamental importance in the theory of strongly correlated electrons, the nature of the ground state of the two-dimensional doped Hubbard model remains intensely debated. Variational approaches provide a powerful route to this problem, but their conclusions can depend sensitively on the chosen wave-function parameterization, the mean-field initialization, or the pinning fields used to guide the optimization, as well as on boundary conditions. This can favor one type of symmetry breaking over another, making it difficult to distinguish the genuine interplay of intertwined or competing orders from biases induced by the variational parameterization. Here, we introduce the Symmetry-Preserving Backflow Pairing (SBP) ansatz, a neural-network wave function that respects translational symmetry by construction and thereby avoids these broken-symmetry minima. The SBP ansatz reaches state-of-the-art variational energies for the $t$-$t'$ Hubbard model on lattices up to $24\times24$ with $504$ electrons, below those of competing pure stripe solutions. By extrapolating to the thermodynamic limit, we find robust evidence for $d$-wave superconducting order, resolving a long-standing question about the $1/8$-doped model at $t'/t=-0.2$ and $U/t=8.0$. Built on general principles of symmetry and locality, the SBP wave function provides a broadly applicable variational representation for challenging interacting fermionic systems.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces the Symmetry-Preserving Backflow Pairing (SBP) ansatz, a neural-network wave function that enforces translational symmetry by construction, avoiding broken-symmetry minima in variational studies of the two-dimensional doped Hubbard model. Applied to the t-t' Hubbard model on lattices up to 24×24 with 504 electrons, it achieves state-of-the-art variational energies and provides robust evidence for d-wave superconducting order at 1/8 doping with t'/t=-0.2 and U/t=8.0.
AI.motivation: The ground state of the two-dimensional doped Hubbard model remains debated, and variational approaches are sensitive to wave-function parameterization, mean-field initialization, pinning fields, and boundary conditions, which can bias results toward certain symmetry-breaking patterns. A symmetry-preserving variational framework is needed to distinguish genuine order from parameterization-induced biases.
AI.method: The authors introduce the SBP ansatz, a neural-network wave function that enforces translational symmetry by construction. It combines backflow transformations with pairing structures, and is applied to the t-t' Hubbard model on large lattices (up to 24×24 with 504 electrons), with thermodynamic-limit extrapolations to characterize the ground-state order.
AI.result: The SBP ansatz achieves state-of-the-art variational energies, surpassing competing pure stripe solutions. Extrapolation to the thermodynamic limit yields robust evidence for d-wave superconducting order at 1/8 doping for t'/t=-0.2 and U/t=8.0, resolving a long-standing question about the nature of the ground state in this regime.
AI.conclusion: Built on general principles of symmetry and locality, the SBP wave function provides a broadly applicable variational representation for challenging interacting fermionic systems, offering a bias-free approach to studying correlated electron physics.

title: Natural van der Waals silicates as hosts for telecom quantum emitters: the case of erbium-doped talc
summary: Erbium ion is among the most promising solid-state single photon emitters and spin-photon interfaces for quantum networks, emitting directly in the telecom C-band in many host semiconductors. Recently, the search for scalable, low-noise host materials turned toward atomically thin and van der Waals materials that enable efficient integration with nanophotonic architectures. Here, we identify talc, a naturally occurring layered magnesium silicate, as a promising host for telecom-active erbium centers. Using first-principles density functional theory combined with multireference wavefunction calculations, we investigate the thermodynamic stability, electronic structure, crystal-field splitting, and optical transitions of erbium-related defects in talc. We find that substitutional incorporation of Er at Mg sites is energetically favourable over a wide range of Fermi-levels, leading predominantly to telecom C band emitting Er$^{3+}$ configuration. The characteristic ${^4}I_{13/2} \rightarrow {^4}I_{15/2}$ transition of Er$^{3+}$ is preserved in the talc environment and remains centred near 1.55 $μ$m, while crystal-field interactions produce a Stark manifold suitable for spectrally selective optical addressing. The combination of thermodynamic stability, wide band gap, low background emission, and compatibility with van der Waals heterostructures suggests that erbium-doped talc constitutes a promising platform for integrated photonics in the C-band.

AI.tldr: This paper identifies talc, a natural layered magnesium silicate, as a promising van der Waals host for telecom C-band erbium single-photon emitters. Using DFT and multireference wavefunction calculations, the authors show that Er substitution at Mg sites is thermodynamically favorable, preserves the characteristic 1.55 μm Er³⁺ transition, and offers a wide band gap, low background emission, and compatibility with van der Waals heterostructures for integrated quantum photonics.
AI.motivation: The search for scalable, low-noise host materials for erbium-based telecom single-photon emitters has moved toward atomically thin and van der Waals materials to enable efficient integration with nanophotonic architectures. Erbium ions emit directly in the telecom C-band in many semiconductors, making them ideal for quantum networks, but identifying suitable low-noise layered hosts remains a key challenge.
AI.method: First-principles density functional theory (DFT) combined with multireference wavefunction calculations were used to investigate the thermodynamic stability, electronic structure, crystal-field splitting, and optical transitions of erbium-related defects in talc (a layered magnesium silicate).
AI.result: Substitutional incorporation of Er at Mg sites in talc is energetically favorable over a wide range of Fermi levels, predominantly yielding the Er³⁺ configuration that emits in the telecom C-band. The characteristic ⁴I₁₃/₂ → ⁴I₁₅/₂ transition is preserved near 1.55 μm, and crystal-field interactions produce a Stark manifold suitable for spectrally selective optical addressing.
AI.conclusion: Erbium-doped talc combines thermodynamic stability, a wide band gap, low background emission, and van der Waals heterostructure compatibility, suggesting it constitutes a promising platform for integrated photonics and quantum networks in the telecom C-band.

title: Is the Aharonov-Casher phase geometrical or dynamical?
summary: We consider two two-dimensional (2D) electronic systems in the presence of a perpendicular homogeneous electric field that generates a Rashba spin-orbit interaction (RSOI): a system of non-interacting electrons in a 2D conductor, modeled using the 2D Schrödinger equation (SE), and a single-layer graphene system, modeled using a 2D Dirac equation (DE) for massless fermions. In both cases the RSOI is expressed via an $SU(2)$ Rashba vector potential ${\bf A}_{R}$. We demonstrate that ${\bf A}_{R}$ cannot be eliminated from either the 2D SE or the 2D DE via a gauge transformation. Nevertheless, for a plane wave solution, an $SU(2)$ matrix exists that eliminates ${\bf A}_{R}$ from the resulting 1D SE. This unitary matrix is an Aharonov-Casher (AC) phase factor, and facilitates the calculation of the AC phase in the Schrödinger scheme. The plane wave solution for the DE contains two components of ${\bf A}_{R}$: $A_{R, k}$ in the direction of the wave vector ${\bf k}$, and $A_{R, n}$ normal to ${\bf k}$. The latter generates an effective electron mass that cannot be eliminated from the DE. The former generates an AC phase that can be eliminated by a time-dependent unitary transformation. Thus, the Dirac AC phase is time-dependent, i.e., it is a dynamical phase. This is in contradistinction to the Schrödinger AC phase which is geometrical.

AI.tldr: This paper analyzes Rashba spin-orbit interaction (RSOI) expressed as an SU(2) vector potential in two 2D systems: a Schrödinger-based 2D conductor and a Dirac-based single-layer graphene. It shows that while the Rashba vector potential cannot be eliminated via gauge transformation from the full 2D equations, it can be eliminated from 1D plane-wave reductions using an Aharonov-Casher (AC) phase factor. In the Schrödinger case the AC phase is geometric, whereas in the Dirac case it is a time-dependent dynamical phase, and a component of the Rashba potential normal to the wave vector generates an unremovable effective electron mass.

title: Boundary phases and thermodynamics of the Kondo spin-$s$ chain: from overscreened Kondo to boundary-bound states
summary: We study a spin-$\frac12$ impurity coupled to the boundary of a strongly correlated spin-$s$ Takhtajan--Babujian chain, an integrable model whose low-energy physics is described by a perturbed $SU(2)_{2s}$ Wess--Zumino--Witten conformal field theory. While boundary conformal field theory determines the low-energy universality class of the weak-coupling regime, exact Bethe Ansatz methods reveal a sequence of boundary quantum phase transitions in which impurity-bound states emerge and reorganize the Hilbert space into multiple excitation towers built on distinct boundary configurations. Weak antiferromagnetic coupling realizes the overscreened $2s$-channel Kondo universality class, whereas stronger couplings generate localized boundary modes and qualitatively new screening mechanisms. To describe the resulting thermodynamics, we develop a generalized thermodynamic Bethe Ansatz framework that captures the multi-tower structure across all regimes. The impurity entropy reproduces the boundary conformal field theory prediction in the overscreened Kondo regime but develops pronounced nonmonotonic temperature dependence once boundary-bound states appear, in quantitative agreement with large-scale finite-temperature matrix-product-operator simulations. Complementary dynamical calculations reveal sharp threshold features in the impurity spectral function that directly track the underlying tower structure. Together, boundary conformal field theory, exact Bethe Ansatz, generalized thermodynamic Bethe Ansatz, and tensor-network simulations provide a unified description of impurity screening, boundary-bound-state formation, and excitation-tower reconstruction in a correlated spin-$s$ chain.

title: Local and quasilocal conservation laws of three-state IRF cellular automata and their quantum deformations

title: The nature of the "pseudogap" in the insulating phase of highly disordered superconductors
summary: Disordered thin films undergoing a superconductor-insulator transition provide a controlled setting for studying pseudogap physics in the absence of competing electronic orders.
